Agent demos show a request going in and a result coming out. What they rarely show is what happens when a step times out halfway and the framework retries it. If that step sent an email, filed a ticket or moved money, a naive retry does it twice. Idempotency, the property that repeating an action produces the same result as doing it once, is invisible when it works and very expensive when it does not.

I ran into this while building systems with real side effects, from on-chain workflows to tools that touch payment runs. Networks drop connections. Model providers return errors after partially completing a call. An agent loop that resumes from a checkpoint may replay the last tool call because it never received confirmation. None of these failures is rare at scale, and each one turns a single intended action into a duplicate that someone has to unwind by hand.

The fixes are old ideas from distributed systems. Give every action a unique request key and have the tool refuse to execute the same key twice. Separate deciding to act from acting, so the decision can be retried freely while the action is guarded. Record completed actions in a ledger the agent checks before doing anything with consequences. None of this involves the model at all, which is exactly why it is easy to forget.

I think idempotency is a good example of why agent engineering is mostly systems engineering. The model decides what should happen, but the surrounding code decides whether it happens once, twice or not at all. Teams that treat agents as clever prompts tend to discover this in production. Teams that treat them as distributed systems with a reasoning component tend to design for it from the beginning.

title: Prompts Deserve Diffs Like Any Other Code
body:
For a long time I edited prompts the way most people do: in place, in a text box, whenever an output looked wrong. Then I noticed that a small wording change meant to fix one case had quietly broken three others, and I had no record of what the prompt used to say. That was the moment I started treating prompts as source code, with version control, review and the same discipline I would give any function.

A prompt is a behavioral specification for a component that cannot be unit tested in the usual way. Changing one sentence can shift output format, tone, refusal behavior and accuracy at the same time. Without a diff, there is no way to connect a change in behavior to a change in instructions. With a diff, a regression becomes a question with an answer: which line changed, and which outputs changed with it.

In practice this means a few simple habits. Prompts live in files, not inline strings scattered through the codebase. Every change is committed with a note on what problem it was meant to fix. A small set of saved inputs gets rerun after each change, and the outputs are compared side by side. It is not elaborate, but it turns prompt editing from guesswork into something closer to engineering.

The underlying point is that natural language does not exempt a component from software discipline. If anything, it needs more, because its failure modes are subtle and its behavior is harder to predict. The teams I have seen struggle with AI reliability usually have excellent practices for their code and none for their prompts, even though the prompts often carry more of the system’s actual logic.

title: Building a Market Console With No Backend
body:
DeepBook Market OS combines spot, margin and prediction markets on Sui into a single console, and it runs entirely on live on-chain data with no backend of its own. That was a deliberate constraint, not a shortcut. Every number on the screen is read directly from the chain, which means there is no private database that could drift from the truth and no server I have to keep alive for the product to work.

The constraint forced better design decisions than I expected. Without a backend to precompute aggregates, I had to think carefully about what the console actually needs to show and how to derive it efficiently from public state. Without mock inputs, every edge case in the real markets showed up immediately, including thin order books and stale prices. The product could not look better than the data, which kept it honest.

It also changes the trust model. A typical trading dashboard asks users to believe that the company behind it is reporting market data faithfully. A client that reads the chain directly lets anyone verify what they see against the same public source. For financial interfaces, that property matters more than polish. The most valuable thing a market tool can offer is confidence that the numbers are not curated.

I think the no-backend pattern is underrated beyond crypto. Many internal tools carry a database whose only purpose is to cache data that already exists in an authoritative system somewhere else, and that cache becomes a second source of truth that slowly diverges. Reading from the source directly is often slower to build and occasionally slower to run, but it removes an entire category of reconciliation problems before they start.

title: Smart Contracts Make You Write Down the Rules You Were Hiding
body:
The Adaptive Funding Engine is a scholarship and grant system on Sui where payouts change with performance. Recipients earn bonuses for early delivery, lose value for delays, and unused funds recycle to waitlisted applicants. Writing those rules as Move smart contracts taught me something I had not expected: most funding programs run on rules nobody has written down precisely, and code does not let you leave them vague.

A human committee can say that delays will be handled case by case. A contract has to specify exactly how much value a recipient loses per day late, when the clock starts, and what happens at the boundary. Every ambiguity becomes a design decision. Several times I realized the fair answer was not obvious, and the discomfort of choosing was a sign that the original program had simply been deferring those decisions to whoever happened to be reviewing.

The recycling rule was the clearest case. In most grant programs, unspent money sits idle or gets returned at the end of a cycle, while qualified applicants wait. Encoding a path from unused funds to the waitlist forced me to define what unused means, how long to wait before reallocating, and who goes next. Each answer is debatable, but at least it is visible and the same for everyone.

I think this is the underappreciated value of putting logic into code, whether on a blockchain or not. It makes implicit policy explicit, and explicit policy can be criticized and improved. Opaque discretion feels flexible, but it often hides inconsistency. A rule written precisely may be imperfect, yet it is applied identically to every recipient, and its flaws are there for anyone to read and argue with.

title: Small Models for Narrow Jobs
body:
PitMind and MatchMind both run on IBM Granite models rather than the largest frontier systems available. People sometimes assume that was a budget decision. It was partly that, but mostly it was a fit decision. Each app asks the model to do a narrow, well-specified job: explain a strategy decision from telemetry, or check whether a claim about a match is supported by the evidence. For narrow jobs, a smaller model is often the better engineering choice.

Smaller models are faster, which matters when an explanation needs to appear alongside live data. They are cheaper to call repeatedly, which matters when a second validation pass doubles the number of calls. And their behavior is easier to constrain, because there is less general capability pulling the output toward creative answers. In a hallucination-sensitive context, a model with fewer ideas of its own can actually be an advantage.

The trade-off is that small models need more structure around them. They depend on well-shaped inputs, explicit instructions and output formats that leave little room for drift. That structure is work, but it is work I would want to do anyway, because it is what makes a system testable. A large model can hide a sloppy pipeline behind fluent output. A small one exposes it immediately, which helps during development.

My rule now is to start with the smallest model that can plausibly do the job and only move up when a specific failure demands it. Defaulting to the biggest model treats capability as free, and it rarely is. It costs latency, money and predictability. Choosing the model to match the task, rather than choosing the task to justify the model, has made every project I have shipped simpler to run.

title: Fallbacks Should Fail Loudly
body:
Most of the AI apps I have deployed have a fallback path for when the model is unavailable, slow or returns something unusable. The question I have learned to ask is not whether a fallback exists, but whether the user can tell when it is active. A fallback that silently substitutes a weaker answer for a stronger one can be worse than an error, because the user keeps trusting output that no longer deserves the same trust.

The temptation to degrade quietly is strong. A visible failure looks bad in a demo, and a smooth experience feels more professional. But when a system switches from a model-generated explanation to a template, or from live data to a cached snapshot, the meaning of what the user sees has changed. If the interface looks identical, the user has no way to adjust how much weight they give it.

So I now mark degraded states explicitly. If data is cached, the screen shows when it was last refreshed. If an AI step was skipped, the output says so. If a validation pass could not run, the result is labeled unverified rather than presented as checked. These labels cost almost nothing to build, and they preserve the one thing a system cannot easily rebuild once lost: the user’s ability to calibrate trust.

I think graceful degradation has been misunderstood as hiding problems. Graceful should mean the system keeps being useful, not that it keeps looking the same. A good fallback lowers its own confidence in public. That honesty is what lets people keep relying on a tool through its bad moments, instead of discovering later that it was guessing while presenting itself as certain. It is a small design habit with an outsized effect on how much people are willing to depend on a tool.

title: Winning in One Day Was Mostly About What We Left Out
body:
Lifeline placed first among forty teams at the Dell and NVIDIA Local AI Hackathon, and it was built end to end in a single day. People ask what the secret was. I think the honest answer is that we spent a surprising amount of the morning deciding what not to build. A one-day deadline does not reward ambition. It rewards a team that agrees early on the smallest version of the idea that still matters.

We had plenty of ideas that would have made Lifeline more impressive on paper: more data sources, more dashboards, more automation. Each one would have added a place for the system to break during the demo. Instead we focused on one complete loop, from damage data to a ranked queue to a human-approved dispatch plan, running locally on a single workstation. A finished loop beats three half-built features every time.

The constraint also clarified what the product was for. When you cannot build everything, you are forced to name the one decision the system supports. For Lifeline, that decision was which collapsed structure a rescue team should go to next, and who approves it. Everything we kept served that question. Everything that did not serve it, however interesting, waited for another day that never needed to come.

I have tried to bring that discipline into longer projects, where it is much harder to hold. With weeks instead of hours, scope expands quietly because there always seems to be time for one more thing. The hackathon taught me to ask, at regular intervals, what the smallest complete version looks like right now, and whether I am building toward it or around it. That single question has saved me more time than any tool I use.

title: Selling Ice Cream in Winter Taught Me to Question the Premise
body:
When I worked on a winter strategy for Far Out Ice Cream, the brief sounded almost like a contradiction. How does an ice cream shop grow during the months when nobody wants ice cream? The obvious answer is to wait for spring. The more useful answer came from questioning what the shop was actually selling. It was not only a cold dessert. It was a place to go, a treat to share, and a brand people liked.

Once the premise shifted, the options multiplied. Affogatos and warm apple crisp kept the product while changing the temperature. A seasonal flavor calendar gave regulars a reason to come back on a schedule. Holiday gift kits turned the brand into something people could give rather than only consume. Culinary school partnerships and a catering launch plan opened channels that do not depend on foot traffic on a cold afternoon.

None of these ideas required inventing a new business. They came from treating the slow season as a design problem rather than a weather problem. The constraint was real, but it applied to one way of selling, not to the relationship the shop had built with its customers. Once I separated those two things, winter looked less like a gap in revenue and more like an underused asset.

I think about that project whenever a situation seems defined by a limitation. The first framing of a problem usually takes the current form of the business as fixed and asks how to survive around the obstacle. The better question is what the business really provides, and whether there is another form of it that the obstacle does not touch. Most constraints are narrower than they first appear.

title: A Loyalty Program Is Only as Good as Its Neighbors
body:
For Kaktus Somabay, a luxury resort on Egypt’s Red Sea coast, I designed a guest experience and loyalty strategy. I expected most of the work to be about points, tiers and rewards. Instead, the part that mattered most was the local partnership ecosystem around the resort. A loyalty program that only rewards guests with more of the same resort feels like a discount. One that connects them to the place feels like a reason to return.

Guests rarely remember a resort for its room upgrade. They remember the dive, the dinner in town, the guide who knew the coast. Most of those experiences sit outside the hotel’s walls and outside its direct control. Building partnerships with local operators let the loyalty program reward guests with access the resort could not provide alone, while sending business to the surrounding community that makes the destination worth visiting.

This changed how I think about competitive advantage in hospitality. A rival resort can copy a points structure in a week. It cannot easily copy a web of relationships with the best local operators, built on trust and repeat business. The boutique retail concept and wellness programming followed the same logic, drawing on the place rather than on generic luxury amenities that any property could install.

The broader lesson I took is that loyalty is rarely built by a single company acting alone. People are loyal to experiences, and experiences usually involve several parties. Designing a program around the whole ecosystem is harder to coordinate, but it produces something competitors struggle to replicate. I now look for that pattern in any strategy problem: where does the real value sit, and who else is already providing part of it?

title: Personas Are Hypotheses, Not Characters
body:
Part of the US market entry strategy I built for Explurger, a gamified travel-social app, was customer persona mapping. Personas have a reputation problem. Too often they become fictional characters with names, hobbies and stock photos, admired in a slide deck and never tested. I tried to treat them differently, as a set of hypotheses about who would adopt the app first and why, each one specific enough to be proven wrong.

A useful persona states a belief that can fail. Instead of describing a traveler who loves adventure, I tried to describe a behavior: someone who already posts trips publicly and would respond to rewards for doing so. That framing connects directly to the conversion funnel. If the persona is right, certain channels and messages should outperform others. If they do not, the persona needs revision, not more decoration.

This mattered especially for the three-phase launch roadmap. Each phase assumed a particular group would carry adoption forward to the next. If the early group was misidentified, every later phase would rest on a broken assumption. Treating personas as hypotheses meant building in early signals that could confirm or challenge them before the larger investments in later phases were committed. A roadmap built on untested personas is really a sequence of bets placed all at once, with no chance to learn between them.

I have come to see this as a general habit worth keeping. Any time a strategy rests on a description of people, the description should be held loosely and tested quickly. Characters are comfortable because they cannot be wrong. Hypotheses are uncomfortable because they can. The discomfort is the point, since it is the only way a plan learns anything from the market it is trying to enter.

title: The Mid-Sized Voice Usually Moves More People
body:
In my research on the GLP-1 weight-loss medication market, one finding kept surprising people who read it: mid-sized creators outperformed headline influencers in conversion. The largest accounts generated reach and attention, but the creators with moderate audiences and closer relationships with their followers moved more people to act. Reach and influence turned out to be different quantities, and the difference was large enough to change where a marketer should spend.

The reason seems to be trust density. A creator with a few hundred thousand engaged followers often speaks to a community that knows them, asks questions and expects honest answers. A massive account speaks to a crowd. When the topic is personal, as health decisions are, people weigh advice from someone who feels like a peer more heavily than advice from someone who feels like a broadcast. The Priority Map and Virality Map made this visible.

I have noticed the same pattern outside marketing, including in my own career. The people who have shaped my decisions most were rarely the most famous voices in finance or AI. They were practitioners with moderate followings who explained their reasoning, answered questions and were specific about what they had actually done. Their audiences were smaller, but their advice was easier to trust and much easier to act on.

So I try to optimize for that kind of influence in my own work. Publishing essays and maintaining projects in public is not about reaching the largest audience possible. It is about being useful and credible to the people who are working on similar problems. A small group that trusts your reasoning is worth more than a large one that has merely seen your name, in marketing and in building a career.

title: A Headline Metric Hides the Work That Earned It
body:
On my portfolio, my internship at The 1525 is summarized by a single figure: four hundred times analyst throughput. It is a striking number, and it is accurate as a headline. But I have learned to be careful with headline metrics, including my own, because a single number compresses away almost everything that made it possible. Most of the real work behind that figure was understanding a process well enough to know which parts could be automated safely.

Automation gains of that scale do not come from clever code alone. They come from mapping how analysts actually spend their time, finding the steps that are repetitive and rule-based, and separating them from the steps that need judgment. Getting that separation wrong produces a tool that is fast and wrong. Getting it right means the automated parts free people to spend more time on the parts that only they can do.

That is also why I value the recommendation from Jason Sizer more than the metric. He described my ability to work through ambiguity and deliver polished work without constant supervision. That description is about process, not output. A throughput figure tells you what happened once. A description of how someone works tells you whether it is likely to happen again in a different setting with different problems.

When I read other people’s portfolios now, I look past headline numbers to the reasoning around them. What was the baseline? What did the person decide not to automate? What did they have to learn about the work first? Those answers say much more about capability than any multiplier. I try to hold my own work to the same standard, and to treat a big number as an invitation to explain, not a substitute for it.

title: What I Noticed Across Fifteen Different Firms
body:
Over forty-two Forage simulations, I worked through tasks modeled on more than fifteen firms, from Goldman Sachs and J.P. Morgan to Lloyds, Standard Chartered, Fidelity International and BCG. Each simulation was short, and none of them made me an expert in that firm. But doing so many in sequence revealed patterns that a single internship would probably not show me, because I could compare how different institutions frame similar problems.

The most consistent pattern was how much the work centered on communication rather than calculation. Whether the task was a credit memo, a client email or a market summary, the analysis was usually the shorter part. The longer part was deciding what the reader needed, in what order, and how much detail they could absorb. Banks, consultancies and asset managers all seemed to value the same thing: conclusions stated clearly before the supporting evidence.

The differences were instructive too. Risk-focused tasks emphasized what could go wrong and how to measure it. Advisory tasks emphasized what a client wanted to achieve. Consulting tasks emphasized structuring an ambiguous problem before solving it. Moving between them taught me that the same financial facts can support very different conclusions depending on the question being asked, and that knowing the question is half of the job.

I would not claim that simulations replace real experience. They are compressed and idealized by design. But as a way to survey an industry before committing to one corner of it, they were valuable. They helped me see which kinds of problems I enjoyed thinking about, and they gave me a vocabulary for talking to people across finance that I would otherwise have built much more slowly. That breadth now helps me decide where depth is worth pursuing.

title: What I Want to Have Shipped Before I Graduate
body:
I graduate from Hult with a BBA in May 2027, and I have started thinking about the time between now and then as a portfolio window rather than a countdown. The question I ask is not what courses I will finish, but what will exist in public by that date that did not exist before. Coursework matters, but it is mostly invisible to anyone outside the classroom. Shipped work is visible, testable and easy to evaluate.

I do not mean a long list of new projects. I already maintain several live apps, and the hidden cost of maintenance is real. The goal is depth over count: projects that are more reliable, better documented and closer to how professionals would actually use them. Tallyhound being open source is part of that. A tool other people can read, run and criticize is worth more than another demo only I understand.

I also want the writing to keep compounding. These essays started as a way to think in public, and over time they have become a record of how my thinking has changed. By graduation, I would like that record to show a clear arc from learning the tools of finance and AI to forming independent judgments about how they should be combined. That arc is harder to fake than any single credential.

Setting goals this way has changed how I spend weeks. When a choice comes up between a new certificate and improving something already live, I tend to choose the improvement. When I am tempted to start something fresh, I ask whether finishing something existing would matter more. Graduation is a fixed date, and treating it as a deadline for useful, public work has made the time ahead feel concrete.

title: My Marketing Classes Made My Finance Tools Usable
body:
I study finance and marketing together, and for a while I treated them as separate tracks: one for building analysis, the other for client strategy work. The more tools I built, the more I realized the marketing side was quietly improving the finance side. Knowing how to model a company is one skill. Knowing how to make someone want to use that model, and understand what it is telling them, is a different one.

The clearest example is how I present output. The Red-Flag Scanner produces a composite score, but the earnings-quality risk card exists because a number alone does not tell a reader what to do. The valuation kit produces a report and a slide deck because different audiences absorb information in different formats. Those decisions came from thinking about audience and message, which is what marketing coursework trains you to do first.

Marketing also taught me to respect the first few seconds of attention. A finance tool that requires reading documentation before it shows anything useful loses most potential users immediately. Leading with a clear result, then letting interested readers drill into the method, is the same structure as a good landing page. I resisted that idea at first because it felt like simplifying, but it turned out to be about prioritizing.

I now think the combination is more valuable than either discipline on its own. Plenty of people can build a correct model, and plenty can craft a persuasive message. Fewer can do both for the same product, which is often where projects succeed or quietly fail. The analysis has to be right, but it also has to reach the person who needs it in a form they will actually use.

title: Awards Are Lagging Indicators
body:
PitMind received the Most Innovative recognition in the IBM SkillsBuild AI Builders Challenge, and I am proud of it. But I have come to think of awards the way an analyst thinks of reported earnings: they are lagging indicators. By the time a project is recognized, the habits that produced it were formed months earlier, through work nobody was judging. The award reports the result. It says much less about what is coming next.

The habits behind PitMind were not glamorous. Learning how Formula 1 telemetry is structured. Building the Driver Soul, Momentum and Race Forecast models one at a time and checking whether their outputs made sense to people who follow the sport. Designing separate Fan and Engineer modes because the two audiences needed different levels of explanation. None of that work felt award-worthy while I was doing it, and most of it was repetitive.

Treating awards as lagging indicators changes how I respond to them. It is tempting to treat recognition as proof that the current approach is right and should be repeated exactly. But the conditions that produced one success rarely repeat. What transfers is the process: choosing a domain I care about, learning it properly and building for a specific user. Those leading indicators are what I try to protect, regardless of outcomes.

I think this applies to any visible milestone in a career, whether an offer, a promotion or a public result. Each one is information about the past. The more useful question is always what I am doing this week that will show up in results a year from now. If the answer is nothing, then the most recent win is already the high point, and no amount of celebrating it will change that.

title: The Bug Was in the Data, Not the Formula
body:
One of the quotes that rotates on my GitHub profile is Warren Buffett’s line that “risk comes from not knowing what you’re doing.” I used to read it as advice about picking stocks. Building the Red-Flag Scanner taught me it applies just as much to the tools that do the picking. The most serious defect I found in the scanner was not in any formula. It was in data I assumed I understood.

Some companies tagged certain SEC filing fields differently from others, and the parser was reading those nonstandard tags without complaint. The result was a handful of health scores that looked plausible but were wrong. Rechecking the Altman or Beneish formulas would never have found the problem, because the formulas were fine. What found it was reconciling the data at each stage: raw filing, cleaned value, model input. The error showed up as a gap between the first two.

That experience changed where I spend my checking time. My instinct had been to audit the clever part of the system, the eleven models and the composite score. Buffett’s line pushed me toward the boring part instead. If I do not know exactly how a number travels from a filing into a ratio, I do not really know what my scanner is measuring, no matter how carefully the math was written.

I now treat reconciliation as the first test, not the last. Before I trust any output, I want to be able to trace one company’s score back through its ratios to the exact source field. That traceability is what the scanner promises reviewers, and it is also what protects me from myself. Knowing what you are doing, in practice, mostly means knowing where your inputs came from and what happened to them along the way.

title: The Price of Waiting for Confirmation
body:
John Bogle’s line that “time is your friend; impulse is your enemy” sits on my quote list under markets, and I follow it most directly in a design choice inside the Red-Flag Scanner. A company is not flagged because one model looks bad. A flag requires several independent models to agree. That rule exists to stop me from reacting to a single noisy reading, which is exactly the kind of impulse Bogle warns against.

The rule has a cost, and I think it is worth being honest about it. Convergence suppresses false alarms, but it adds lag. The Altman Z-Score often flags a company only after its accruals gap has been widening for years. By the time enough models agree, some of the information has already been priced. Patience protects me from noise, but it also means I am sometimes late to a signal that was real from the start.

My answer has been to separate early warning from conclusion. The accruals gap tends to move before the solvency models react, so the scanner treats it as a reason to look closer rather than as a verdict. Convergent red flags generate a manual analysis card. A single early signal earns attention, not action. That split lets me be patient about decisions without being blind to what is changing underneath.

I think this is what Bogle’s advice looks like in a working tool. Time is a friend only if you use the waiting period to gather evidence, not just to sit still. Impulse is an enemy because it confuses one reading with a pattern. The discipline is in building a process where early signals change where I look while only converging evidence changes what I conclude, and in accepting the lag that comes with that.

title: Arithmetic You Can Rerun
body:
Benjamin Graham’s advice to “buy not on optimism, but on arithmetic” is one of the quotes I see most often on my profile, and it shaped a specific decision in the Orcen Capital valuation kit. The entire 84-sheet model is generated from a single YAML configuration file and versioned in git. Change an input, rerun it, and every sheet recalculates identically. That is my version of making arithmetic, not mood, the thing that decides.

Optimism hides in spreadsheets in quiet ways. A growth rate gets nudged in one tab and not another. A hardcoded number survives three revisions because nobody remembers why it is there. After a few weeks, the model reflects a series of small hopeful edits rather than a set of stated assumptions. Putting every assumption in one config file forces each one into the open, where it can be read, questioned and changed deliberately.

Version control adds the other half. If my fair value moves, I can see exactly which assumption moved it and when. That turns an argument about whether a stock is attractive into a narrower argument about a specific input. It also means I cannot quietly rewrite history. The record shows what I believed at each point, which is uncomfortable in the best possible way, and exactly the point.

I do not think Graham meant that arithmetic removes judgment. Every input in the config is still a judgment call. What reproducibility does is keep those judgments honest by making them visible and repeatable. If two people run the same file and get the same answer, they can argue productively about the inputs. If the answer depends on who touched the spreadsheet last, the arithmetic is decoration on top of optimism.

title: My Old Price Target Is Not Evidence
body:
Buffett has a line on my quote list that I find more uncomfortable every time it comes around: “Forecasts may tell you a great deal about the forecaster; they tell you nothing about the future.” When I wrote up the uncertainty behind the Orcen Capital kit, one source I named was that analysts anchor on narratives and on their own prior targets. I wrote that sentence knowing it describes me as much as anyone.

The pattern is subtle. Once I have published a fair value, every new piece of information gets measured against it. Good news confirms the target. Bad news looks temporary. The number I wrote down weeks ago starts acting like evidence, even though it was only ever my estimate built on assumptions that may no longer hold. Buffett’s point is that the forecast describes my thinking at the time, not the company.

The kit’s response is structural rather than motivational. It generates the valuation from current inputs each run instead of adjusting a previous result, and it presents a range with the spread between methods rather than a single tidy number. When the methods diverge, the divergence is flagged rather than averaged away. That makes it harder for an old point estimate to survive simply because I am attached to it.

The rule I am trying to adopt outside the model is to write down what has changed about a company before I look at my old number. If I look first, the old number frames everything that follows. Reading Buffett’s line this way turns it from a cynical joke about forecasters into a practical instruction: treat your own past predictions as information about yourself, and rebuild the view from the facts in front of you.

title: A Screen Decides Where the Two Hours Go
body:
Peter Drucker’s distinction that “efficiency is doing things right; effectiveness is doing the right things” helped me explain what the screening pipeline I built at The 1525 actually did. Before it, reviewing a company took an analyst roughly two hours. The pipeline made it possible to screen more than two thousand companies in about ten hours. That is the efficiency part, and it produced the headline figure of four hundred times throughput.

The effectiveness part is less visible but more important. The point of the screen was never to replace the two hours of careful review. It was to decide which companies deserved them. A manual, analyst-by-analyst process spends the same time on a weak candidate as on a strong one. An automated first pass surfaces the names worth a closer look, so the expensive human attention goes where it is most likely to matter.

Building it required being clear about which parts of the review were mechanical and which needed judgment. Ratios, thresholds and data pulls are mechanical and safe to automate. Reading a business model, weighing management and deciding whether a story holds together are not. If I had automated the judgment, the tool would have been efficient and wrong. Keeping those parts separate is what made the speed useful.

I think Drucker’s line is a good test for any automation project in finance. Speed is easy to measure and easy to celebrate, but faster review of the wrong companies is no improvement. The real question is whether the tool changes what people spend their time on. A screen that moves the two hours from random names to promising ones has done something more valuable than any throughput multiple can capture.

title: Reconciliation Is the Oldest Control
body:
Henry Ford’s line that “quality means doing it right when no one is looking” is on my quote list under efficiency, and the first place I practiced it was behind a counter, not a keyboard. At a Western Union sub-agency in Guatemala City, I managed daily cash operations of up to fifteen thousand quetzales and handled around fifty transactions a day. At the end of each shift, the cash had to match the records exactly.

Reconciliation is unglamorous, and it is also one of the oldest controls in finance. Nobody watches you count the drawer. Nobody notices when the numbers match. The only time anyone pays attention is when they do not, and by then the problem has usually compounded. Doing it carefully every day, when nothing seems wrong, is what makes the rare discrepancy easy to find instead of a mystery.

I improved service speed by about ten percent there, and it came from making reconciliation more efficient rather than skipping it. That distinction matters. The tempting shortcut is to trust the system and check less. The better path is to make checking fast enough that it never feels like a reason to cut corners. Quality that depends on having spare time is not quality, it is luck.

I see the same principle in every tool I have built since. The Red-Flag Scanner reconciles raw filings to model inputs. Tallyhound checks every quoted line against the source file. Both are versions of counting the drawer. Ford’s line reminds me that the controls that matter most are the ones that run quietly every day, done properly whether or not anyone will ever review them. That is the standard I learned at the counter, and it still applies to every model I ship.

title: Watching a DCF Move Showed Me Where Value Is Fragile
body:
Seth Klarman wrote that “risk is not inherent in an investment; it is always relative to the price paid.” I understood the sentence long before I felt it. What made it concrete was building an animation with Manim showing how a DCF valuation moves as the discount rate and terminal growth change. Seeing the value bend, rather than reading a sensitivity table, changed how I think about the price I would be willing to pay.

The animation makes one thing obvious: the relationship is not linear. As the discount rate moves closer to the terminal growth rate, small changes in either input produce enormous swings in value. Near that edge, a valuation that looked precise becomes almost meaningless. A table shows the same numbers, but the motion shows the shape, and the shape is where the risk lives.

That is where Klarman’s point connects. If I pay a price that only makes sense under optimistic inputs near that fragile region, I am taking much more risk than the base case suggests, even if the company itself is excellent. If I pay a price that holds up across a wide band of reasonable assumptions, the same company becomes a much safer investment. The business did not change. My exposure to being wrong did.

I now ask a specific question of every valuation I build: where on the curve does the current price sit? If justifying it requires inputs from the steep part, the investment is fragile regardless of how good the story is. Visualizing the model did not make me better at forecasting. It made me better at seeing how much of my answer depends on assumptions I can least afford to get wrong.

title: If I Can’t State the Thesis in a Sentence, I Don’t Own It
body:
Peter Lynch’s advice to “know what you own, and know why you own it” is one of the shortest quotes on my list and one of the hardest to follow. Working through investment analysis in simulations at Fidelity International and Goldman Sachs, I noticed how easily equity research turns into a long list of facts about a company without ever answering the question a portfolio manager actually needs answered: why this, and why now?

The test I try to hold myself to is simple. Before I write anything detailed, I try to state the thesis in one sentence that a reader could disagree with. Not a description of the business, but a claim: the market is underestimating how long this margin can last, or the balance sheet risk is priced as if it were permanent. If I cannot write that sentence, I do not understand the investment yet, however many pages of analysis I have.

The sentence also tells me what to monitor. If the thesis is about margin durability, then the quarterly numbers that matter are the ones that test it, and the rest is noise. Without a clear reason for owning something, every headline feels relevant, and it becomes easy to hold a position long after the original argument has quietly stopped being true.

I think Lynch’s line is really about accountability to yourself. Knowing why you own something means knowing what would make you wrong. That is what turns research from a collection of opinions into a decision you can review later. The habit carries into how I build tools too: every output in my valuation work ties back to the assumption that produced it, so the reason is never separated from the result.

title: Margin Turns Being Right Into Being Early
body:
One line on my quote list, credited there to A. Gary Shilling and often attributed to Keynes, reads: “Markets can remain irrational a lot longer than you and I can remain solvent.” I thought about it constantly while building DeepBook Market OS, which brings spot, margin and prediction markets on Sui into one console. Putting margin next to spot on the same screen made the difference between the two very hard to ignore.

In a spot position, being right eventually is usually enough. If the price moves against you, you can wait. With leverage, timing becomes part of the thesis. A position can be correct about where a price is going and still be liquidated on the way there, because the path matters as much as the destination. The console shows live on-chain data, and thin order books make that path far bumpier than any chart suggests.

That changes how I think about conviction. Strong conviction tempts people to increase size, and leverage is the easiest way to do it. But the stronger my view, the more I should worry about whether I can survive being early. Solvency is what buys the time for an idea to work. Leverage spends that time in advance, often without the trader noticing until it is gone.

I take Shilling’s line as a sizing rule rather than a market prediction. It says nothing about whether markets are rational. It says that my ability to stay in a position has a limit, and that limit is set by my balance sheet, not by how confident I feel. Building the console made that concrete: every margin feature I added was really a question about how long a user could afford to be right too soon.

title: Personal Finance Is Where Patience Gets Priced
body:
Buffett describes the stock market as “a device for transferring money from the impatient to the patient,” and it is one of six quotes on my list tagged patience. The course that made the line feel personal was not a valuation class. It was an introductory personal finance course on Coursera covering budgeting, saving, investing, debt and credit. It reminded me that patience is not only an investing virtue. It is a number you can calculate.

Compounding is the clearest example. The same monthly saving produces very different outcomes depending on when it starts, and the difference comes almost entirely from time rather than effort. Debt works the same way in reverse. High-interest balances compound against you, quietly transferring money from the impatient borrower to the patient lender. Seeing both sides in one course made Buffett’s line feel less like a slogan and more like arithmetic.

It also changed how I think about my own trade-offs as a student. Spending now versus investing in skills, taking a quick opportunity versus building toward a better one, these decisions have a compounding structure too. The returns on building real projects or learning a difficult tool show up slowly, then all at once. Impatience usually means trading a large future gain for a small present comfort.

What I appreciate about personal finance is that it strips investing down to behavior. There are no clever models, only habits sustained over long periods. Most of the wealth-building advice that works is simple and hard at the same time. Buffett’s line explains why: the difficult part is never knowing what to do, it is continuing to do it while the reward is still years away and nothing seems to be happening.

title: Test the Approval Chain That Breaks Halfway
body:
Edsger Dijkstra’s observation that “testing can show the presence of bugs but never their absence” is one of sixteen building quotes on my GitHub profile, and it shaped how I tested OpsFlow, my policy-bound AI operations agent on Sui. A clean demo proves almost nothing about an agent that moves money. What matters is how it behaves in the cases nobody shows on stage, where something goes wrong halfway through.

So I probed those cases deliberately. An approval chain that breaks after the first approver signs. A payment request just outside the authorized range. A vendor that is not on the approved list but looks similar to one that is. In each case, the question was not whether the model would notice. It was whether the deterministic policy layer would block the action even if the model tried to talk its way past it.

Dijkstra’s point kept me humble about the results. Passing those tests did not prove OpsFlow was safe. It proved that the specific failures I could imagine were handled. That is why the design does not rely on testing alone. The model only proposes an action plan, and Move smart contracts enforce the limits, so even failures I never imagined are contained by rules the model cannot override.

I think this is the right relationship between testing and architecture for any agent with real consequences. Tests find the bugs you can think of. Architecture limits the damage from the ones you cannot. If an agent’s safety depends entirely on how thoroughly it was tested, it is only as safe as its designer’s imagination. Bounding what it can do in the first place is what lets testing be useful instead of reassuring.

title: A Ranked List Reads as Authority
body:
Charlie Munger said that “knowing what you don’t know is more useful than being brilliant,” and the clearest application I have found for it came from Lifeline, the search-and-rescue triage system my team built at the Dell and NVIDIA Local AI Hackathon. Our first version produced a ranked list of collapsed structures and stopped there. Looking at it, we realized something uncomfortable: a ranked list reads as authority whether or not it has earned it.

Every input behind that ranking was a proxy. Satellite damage grading describes the outside of a building, not who is alive inside. Life-sign sensing is sparse and noisy, and silent for reasons unrelated to whether anyone is there. A clean ordered list hides all of that. A commander looking at position one and position two has no way to know whether the gap between them is meaningful or an artifact of weak data.

So the design question changed from how to rank better to how to make the ranking state what it does not know. The system surfaces each ranking as a decision aid rather than a verdict, and it is explicit about which inputs are live sensor data and which were simulated for the demo. That is Munger’s advice translated into an interface: the limits of the knowledge travel with the answer.

I think this matters well beyond disaster response. Any AI output presented in a confident format inherits authority from the format itself, whether a ranked list, a score or a polished paragraph. Brilliance in the model does not fix that. What fixes it is honesty about uncertainty, built into how results are shown. The more consequential the decision, the more important it is that the system admits what it cannot see.

title: Provenance Is a Receipt for Creative Work
body:
Linus Torvalds’ line “Talk is cheap. Show me the code.” is on my quote list as a building principle, and I think it describes the problem StoryForge was built to address. StoryForge is a cryptographic provenance ledger for AI-assisted creative work, one of the projects I built in the IBM SkillsBuild cohort alongside PitMind and MatchMind. As AI tools spread into writing and design, claims about who made what become cheap. Records become valuable.

Today, anyone can say a piece of work is original, or that AI was used only lightly, or that a draft existed before a competing one. Without evidence, those claims are just talk. A provenance ledger replaces assertions with records: what was created, when, and through which steps. Cryptographic methods matter because they make those records tamper-evident, so a history cannot be quietly rewritten after the fact to tell a better story.

What interested me about the problem is that it is really an accounting problem wearing creative clothes. Finance solved a version of it long ago with ledgers and audit trails, because money needs a history people can trust. Creative work increasingly needs the same thing. The question is not whether AI was involved, but whether the process can be shown rather than merely described.

I find Torvalds’ line applies to my own work as much as to the people a tool like this serves. Many of my projects come with live demos and public code for the same reason: a claim about what a system does is far weaker than the system itself. Provenance is just that principle applied to authorship. When the record exists and cannot be edited, the talk stops mattering, and the work can speak for itself.

title: Thirty-Nine Thousand Lines Started as One DCF
body:
John Gall observed that “a complex system that works is invariably found to have evolved from a simple system that worked.” When people see the Orcen Capital valuation kit today, they see about thirty-nine thousand lines of Python producing an 84-sheet Excel model, a Word report and a slide deck from one configuration file. What they do not see is that it started as a single discounted cash flow model and nothing else.

That first version worked, in the narrow sense that it produced a number. Building it also showed me its biggest weakness: terminal value was carrying sixty to eighty percent of the answer, which meant the number was mostly an assumption in disguise. That discovery shaped everything that followed. Comparable companies, precedent transactions and an LBO were added as independent cross-checks, and the bias-correction modules came after those.

Each addition answered a problem the previous version had revealed, rather than a feature I imagined in advance. If I had tried to design the whole system from the start, I would have built the wrong pieces, because I did not yet know where the real weaknesses were. The simple version taught me what the complex one needed. Gall’s law is not just a warning; it is a method.

I apply the same approach to AI systems now. I start with the smallest pipeline that produces a real output, run it until it breaks in an informative way, then add the component that addresses that break. It is slower to impress anyone this way. But every part of the final system has a reason to exist, and when something fails, I usually know which layer it came from because I watched each one arrive.

title: Make It Work Before You Make It Smart
body:
Kent Beck’s sequence, “make it work, make it right, make it fast,” is one of the building quotes on my list, and Tallyhound follows a version of it that I would phrase slightly differently: make it work before you make it smart. The free public demo of my audit console runs on fixed rules, and the version with local AI agents switched on is the one people can sign up to hear about.

That order was deliberate. Fixed rules already catch a large share of accounts payable problems: payments made twice under re-keyed invoice numbers, split orders, unverified bank detail changes, large payments to brand-new vendors. These patterns are well defined, and rules catch them reliably and cheaply. Starting with the rules meant the tool was useful on day one, without depending on a model being available, fast or right.

The AI layer then has a clear job: propose findings the rules miss, with every quoted line checked against the source file and a Skeptic agent trying to disprove each one. Because the rule-based core already works, I can measure what the agents add rather than guessing. If they produce noise, the tool still functions. If they produce real findings, the improvement is visible against a working baseline.

I think many AI products invert Beck’s order and pay for it. They start with the model because it is the exciting part, then try to make the result reliable afterward. In a domain like audit, reliability is the product. Building the deterministic core first gave me something that worked, then something that was right, and only then something that was clever. That sequence is less dramatic, but it is much easier to trust, and in audit work trust is the entire point.

title: Resourcefulness on a Single Workstation
body:
Tony Robbins’ line “it’s not about resources, it’s about resourcefulness” sits under motivation on my quote list, but I think of it as an engineering principle because of Lifeline. At the Dell and NVIDIA Local AI Hackathon, where about one hundred fifty builders were selected for a single-day build, the entire reasoning stack of our system ran locally on one Dell Pro Max workstation. No cloud calls, no external APIs, no keys.

That constraint fit the problem. After an earthquake, connectivity is exactly what cannot be assumed. A triage system that depends on a remote model fails at the moment it is needed most. Running inference locally through Ollama meant Lifeline could keep working in the conditions it was designed for. The limit on resources was not something to work around. It was a requirement of the use case.

It also forced sharper choices. With one machine, every model call had a cost in time, so we could not afford wasteful steps or redundant reasoning. Parts of the problem that had exact solutions, like routing, went to Google OR-Tools rather than to a model. The constraint pushed us toward an architecture where each component did only what it was best at, which made the whole system faster and easier to explain.

I have come to see local-first AI as an underrated design choice, especially for sensitive or high-stakes work. It removes a dependency, keeps data on the device and makes cost predictable. Robbins’ line fits because the interesting work happens when you stop asking for more compute and start asking what the smallest reliable system looks like. Constraints like that are often where the best engineering decisions come from, and Lifeline was the clearest proof I have of that.

title: Agent Graphs Should Fit in One Head
body:
Dijkstra wrote that “the competent programmer is fully aware of the limited size of his own skull.” It is my favorite building quote, and it explains why I use LangGraph for agent work instead of letting an agent loop freely. A graph makes the possible paths explicit: which step can follow which, where state is stored and where a human checkpoint sits. I can read the whole flow and hold it in my head.

Free-running agent loops are impressive in demos and very hard to reason about in practice. When the model decides at each step what to do next, the space of possible behaviors grows faster than anyone can review. A bug becomes a question about an unrepeatable conversation. With an explicit graph, the same bug becomes a question about one node and one transition, which is something a person can actually inspect, test and fix with confidence.

Keeping graphs small is the second half of the discipline. When a workflow grows to the point that I cannot sketch it from memory, that is usually a sign it should be split into smaller graphs with clear handoffs. The limit is not the framework. It is my own capacity to understand what I have built, which is exactly the constraint Dijkstra was pointing at.

I think this is one of the most underrated principles in agent engineering. Teams worry about whether the model is smart enough, but the more common failure is that the system around it has grown too complex for its builders to understand. A model can be replaced with a better one. A system nobody can reason about can only be rewritten, usually after it has already caused a problem nobody could predict.

title: Stop Asking Whether the Agent Understands
body:
One of the quotes on my list is Dijkstra’s remark that “the question of whether a computer can think is no more interesting than whether a submarine can swim.” It has become a practical rule for how I evaluate AI systems. Whether a model really understands a balance sheet or a race strategy is a fascinating debate. It is also almost useless when deciding whether to trust its output in a specific task.

The useful questions are functional. Does the output match the evidence? Does it fail in predictable ways? Does it hold up on inputs it has not seen? In MatchMind, I did not try to prove the model understood football. I built checks that label each explanation as verified or unverified against the underlying data. That label answers a question a user can act on, which the philosophical one never does.

Anthropomorphizing agents creates real engineering risk. When a model writes fluently, people assume it reasons the way a careful person would, and they extend the kind of trust they would give a colleague. That trust is misplaced, not because the model is stupid, but because its failure modes are different from a person’s. It can be right about something hard and wrong about something trivial within the same answer.

So I try to describe my systems in terms of behavior rather than mind. A component retrieves, ranks, summarizes or checks. It does not know or believe. That language keeps evaluation grounded in what can be measured, and it keeps users calibrated about what they are relying on. Dijkstra’s submarine moves through water extremely well. Nobody needs it to swim, and nobody should worry about whether it does. The same goes for the agents I build.

title: Fan Mode Was Built by Taking Things Away
body:
Antoine de Saint-Exupéry wrote that perfection is achieved “not when there is nothing left to add, but when there is nothing left to take away.” PitMind, my Formula 1 strategy platform, has two modes, Engineer and Fan, and the quote describes the difference between them better than any feature list. Engineer mode keeps the depth. Fan mode was designed mostly by deciding what to remove.

Both modes draw on the same 2025 live telemetry and the same three custom models: Driver Soul, Momentum and Race Forecast. An engineer wants the full detail, including the inputs and the uncertainty behind each projection. A fan watching a race wants to know what is happening and why a team might pit now. Showing the fan everything the engineer sees would technically be more complete and practically much less useful.

Subtraction turned out to be harder than addition. Every metric I considered removing seemed important to someone. The test I found most useful was whether a piece of information changed what a fan would understand about the next few laps. If it did not, it moved to Engineer mode. The result was not a simplified product. It was the same analysis expressed at the level of detail its audience could use.

I think AI interfaces especially need this discipline. Models can generate endless detail, and it is tempting to show all of it as proof of sophistication. But an explanation is only useful when the audience can absorb it. Designing the fan experience by taking things away taught me that clarity is not the absence of depth. It is choosing, deliberately, which depth belongs on the screen for the person looking at it. Everything else is still there, one mode away, for whoever needs it.

title: Agent Plans Should Expire
body:
Dwight Eisenhower’s line “plans are worthless, but planning is everything” is one of my favorite building quotes, and Lifeline is where I saw what it means for an AI system. Our triage system produced dispatch plans for rescue teams, but the survivor-likelihood scores behind those plans were continuously re-weighted as new life-sign telemetry came in. A plan that was right ten minutes ago could be wrong now.

That shaped the architecture. Instead of treating a dispatch plan as an output to execute, we treated it as the current best answer under current evidence. When the ranking changed, the routing layer could recompute assignments, and the human commander reviewed the updated plan before authorizing it. The value was not in any single plan. It was in a process that could regenerate a sensible plan quickly whenever the situation shifted.

Many agent designs get this backward. They produce a multi-step plan up front and then execute it faithfully, even as the facts that justified it change underneath. That makes the agent look decisive, but it means the plan quietly goes stale. A better pattern is to attach the assumptions to the plan and replan whenever those assumptions are violated, with a person approving each meaningful change.

I now think every agent plan should carry an implicit expiry: the conditions under which it stops being valid. Eisenhower’s point was that preparation builds understanding, not certainty. For agents, the equivalent is that the planning machinery, including the data feeds, the solver and the approval loop, is the durable asset. Any single plan it produces is temporary by design, and the system should treat it that way. An agent that cannot let go of its own plan is not decisive; it is simply out of date.

title: Why My GitHub Profile Rotates a Quote Every Day
body:
My GitHub profile shows a different quote every day. A small GitHub Action walks through a curated list of 101 quotes, one per day, and wraps back to the start when it reaches the end. The list is organized by theme: building, leadership, risk, persistence, motivation, markets, dedication, efficiency and patience. As I write this, it shows Jim Ryun: “Motivation is what gets you started. Habit is what keeps you going.”

The idea behind it is that good advice rarely fails because people disagree with it. It fails because they forget it at the moment it would have mattered. A quote I read once in a book has almost no effect on what I do next month. The same quote appearing on a page I open regularly, in the middle of actual work, has a much better chance of shaping a decision.

The mix is deliberate. Buffett, Graham and Marks sit next to Dijkstra, Knuth and Kent Beck, and next to Pelé, Bruce Lee and Seneca. That reflects how I work. A valuation model needs Graham’s discipline, the code that generates it needs Dijkstra’s humility, and finishing either one needs the persistence quotes more than I would like to admit. Seeing them rotate together keeps those disciplines connected in my head.

The automation matters too. If I had to choose a quote each morning, I would stop doing it within a week. Making it run on a schedule turned an intention into a habit, which is exactly Ryun’s point. The same Action posts my latest essays below it, so the profile is a small daily record of what I am reading, writing and building. It is a reminder system I cannot forget to use, which is the only kind that has ever worked for me.

title: Deep Work Is Scheduled, Not Scavenged
body:
Jim Ryun’s line that “Motivation is what gets you started. Habit is what keeps you going.” came up on my profile recently, and it describes the first of the three habits I list on my portfolio. I protect a block on my calendar for deep work before the week starts, like a meeting I cannot move. It is not whatever time is left over after classes, applications and outreach. It is decided in advance.

The logic is simple. When deep work depends on motivation, it happens on good days and disappears on busy ones, which means it disappears most weeks. Leftover time is always fragmented. An hour between commitments is enough to answer messages, not enough to build a valuation model or debug an agent workflow. Absorbed, difficult work only shows up reliably when the slot exists before the week has a chance to fill it.

Bruce Lee’s line on my list, “the successful warrior is the average man with laser-like focus,” is the other half of it. A scheduled block only works if it is protected inside as well as outside. That means one problem per block, no inbox and a clear idea before starting of what finished looks like. The calendar creates the space. Focus is what makes the space produce something.

What surprises people is how little time this requires. A few protected blocks a week, held consistently, produce more than scattered hours spent half-working. It is the habit I lean on most for long projects, because sessions decided in advance happen and sessions I hope to find usually do not. Motivation still matters for starting something new. But the habit is what carries a project through the long middle, where nothing about it feels exciting anymore.

title: One Kick Ten Thousand Times
body:
Bruce Lee said, “I fear not the man who has practiced 10,000 kicks once, but I fear the man who has practiced one kick 10,000 times.” It sits under dedication on my quote list, and it describes the third habit on my portfolio, the one I learned from soccer. Treat it like drills, not reading. Fail in public, immediately, then run it again until the movement no longer needs thought.

In finance, that means rebuilding things I think I already understand. I rebuilt the same DCF logic four times in a single month. Not because the first version was broken, but because explaining a model back is a very different skill from reproducing it without notes. My rule is simple: if I cannot rebuild a number from scratch, I do not actually know it yet, however confidently I described it five minutes earlier.

Reading creates a feeling of understanding that is mostly recognition. When I see a completed model, every step looks obvious. When I face a blank sheet, the gaps appear immediately: which cash flow adjustments come first, how working capital enters, where the mid-year convention changes the math. Drilling exposes those gaps in a way that reading about them never does, and each repetition closes a few more.

The soccer comparison holds in another way too. In training, nobody practices a skill once and calls it learned. Repetition is how a movement survives pressure, and finance has its own version of pressure: a deadline, an interview, a client question. Lee’s point is that depth in one thing beats familiarity with many. I would rather rebuild one valuation from memory than have skimmed ten that I could only recognize. That is the whole point of the drill.

title: Rejections Are Data, Not Verdicts
body:
Samuel Beckett’s line “Ever tried. Ever failed. No matter. Try again. Fail again. Fail better.” is on my quote list under persistence, and I think the most important word in it is better. Failing again is easy. Failing better requires learning something from each attempt. That is the idea behind the second habit on my portfolio: I treat rejections as data, not verdicts.

In practice, I track internship applications like a pipeline: sent, screened, interviewed, offered. That structure turns a stream of disappointing emails into something I can analyze. If applications stall at screening, the problem is likely my resume or how I describe my experience. If they stall after interviews, it is something else. A rejection on its own says little. A pattern of rejections at one stage says a lot.

The other part of the habit is timing. When a rejection lands, I rewrite the weak line that same night, while the reason it did not work is still fresh. Waiting a week makes the feedback vague and the motivation weaker. Acting immediately turns a bad moment into a small improvement, which makes the next attempt slightly better than the last. That is what failing better looks like day to day.

I find this approach easier on my mindset too. A rejection treated as a verdict feels like a judgment of my worth. The same rejection treated as data is just a measurement of a process that can be improved. Beckett was not writing about job searches, but his line captures the attitude I want: keep trying, expect to fail, and make sure each failure teaches me something specific. Over enough attempts, those small lessons add up to a much stronger application than talent alone would produce.

title: Making My Impact Last After I Left
body:
Sheryl Sandberg described leadership as “making others better as a result of your presence and making that impact last in your absence.” It is one of thirteen leadership quotes on my list, and the second half of it changed how I think about my internship at The 1525. Building the screening pipeline was the visible part. Teaching the other interns to run it without me was the part that determined whether it would last.

A tool only one person can operate is a liability disguised as an asset. If I had built the pipeline and kept running it myself, the throughput gain would have disappeared the day I left. So I spent time guiding the other interns through how it worked, what its outputs meant and how to run it on their own. The goal was to turn something I had built into something the team could use on its own.

Teaching it also improved the tool. Explaining a pipeline to someone else exposes every assumption that only made sense in my own head. Questions about why a threshold existed or what a flag meant pushed me to make outputs clearer and documentation better. Martin Fowler’s line on my list, that good programmers write code humans can understand, felt very concrete in those conversations.

I think early-career people underestimate this kind of leadership because it carries no title. It would have been easy to treat the pipeline as my personal achievement. But Sandberg’s test is the right one. The measure of work is not how impressive it is while you are present. It is whether the people around you are more capable after you leave. That is the standard I want to keep applying.

title: Strong Without Being Pushy
body:
Jim Rohn wrote that “the challenge of leadership is to be strong, but not rude; be kind, but not weak.” I first understood that balance in sales, not leadership. As a client specialist at SeOnline, I managed the full sales cycle from outreach to close, and I ran the whole relationship remotely. Prospecting, needs assessments, negotiation and closing all happened over chat and video, with clients in both Guatemala and the United States.

Remote selling removes most of the signals people rely on in person. There is no handshake, no shared room and often no body language beyond a video frame. Tone carries much more weight. Push too hard in a message and it reads as aggressive. Stay too soft and the conversation drifts without a decision. Rohn’s balance had to show up in written words and short calls, where every sentence counted.

What helped most was preparation. A tailored proposal built from a real needs assessment let me be firm about value without pressuring anyone, because the case was already specific to their situation. Kindness then meant listening to objections properly rather than talking past them. Strength meant asking for a decision once the fit was clear, instead of hoping the client would volunteer one.

Working across two markets added another layer. Clients in different markets can expect different pacing and directness, and the same message could land very differently with each. Learning to adjust without becoming inconsistent was one of the most useful things that job taught me. Rohn’s line describes a balance I still practice in interviews, client work and team settings: firm on substance, generous in manner. It is harder than either extreme, and far more effective over a long relationship.

title: Every Campaign Is Carried One Small Stone at a Time
body:
Confucius is credited with the line “the man who moves a mountain begins by carrying away small stones,” and it sits under dedication on my quote list. It describes my digital marketing internship at Western Union better than any summary. I reported to the Digital Marketing Director at the central agency in Guatemala, supporting multi-channel campaigns across Central America, from billboards and print to social channels.

The project I remember most clearly was helping organize a Father’s Day event and the process behind it, from distribution through promotion across Western Union’s social channels. From outside, an event like that looks like a single moment. From inside, it is hundreds of small tasks: materials, timing, coordination, approvals and posts that all have to land in the right order. Missing any one of them weakens the whole.

What the internship taught me is that regional brand campaigns are built the same way. Billboard placements, print collateral and social posts each look minor on their own. Their effect comes from consistency across channels and countries over time. No single asset moves the brand. The accumulation does, which means the unglamorous execution work matters as much as the creative idea at the start.

I carry that lesson into my technical projects. A valuation kit or an audit console also looks like one thing from outside and turns out to be thousands of small decisions inside. The Confucius line reassures me on days when progress feels invisible. Carrying one stone at a time is slow, but it is the only way mountains actually move, in marketing, in finance and in code. The internship made that visible to me early, before I had built anything of my own, and I am grateful it did.

title: Changing Direction Before Changing Destination
body:
Jim Rohn said, “You cannot change your destination overnight, but you can change your direction overnight.” It is one of twelve motivation quotes on my list, and it describes how I think about my career right now. On my portfolio, I state the direction plainly: I am most interested in roles that combine agentic AI, robust financial modeling and systems thinking, in AI engineering, fintech or finance teams that want to use modern AI well.

That sentence did not come from a single decision. It came from noticing which projects I kept returning to. The Orcen valuation kit, the Red-Flag Scanner, Tallyhound and OpsFlow all sit at the same intersection: financial judgment encoded in software, with AI used carefully and controls designed around it. The direction became clear once I looked at where my time had already been going. Choices revealed it more honestly than any plan I could have written in advance.

Rohn’s distinction is useful because it removes pressure. I do not need to know exactly which job I will have in five years. I need each week’s choices to point the right way. Picking a project that combines both fields, writing about what I learn and taking courses that close specific gaps are all directional moves, even if none of them is a destination.

It also gives me a practical filter. When an opportunity appears, I ask whether it moves me toward that intersection or away from it. Some good opportunities fail that test, and saying no to them is part of keeping a direction. Destinations change as you learn more about them. A clear direction, followed consistently, tends to produce better destinations than a plan made too early.

title: Patience With Myself While Learning Two Fields
body:
Saint Francis de Sales wrote, “Have patience with all things, but first of all with yourself.” It is one of only six patience quotes on my list, and it is the one I need most. Studying finance and marketing at Hult while building AI systems means I am a beginner in something almost all the time. Every month includes a moment where I understand far less than I want to.

The temptation is to compare my progress in each field with people who focus on only one. A finance student who never codes will know certain accounting details better than I do. An engineer who never studies valuation will know certain frameworks better. Measured against either, I look slow. Measured against the combination, the picture is different, but that comparison is much harder to see from day to day.

Patience with myself does not mean lowering standards. It means expecting the learning curve to be uneven and not treating a hard week as evidence that the approach is wrong. The DCF I rebuilt four times, the scanner bug that only appeared when I reconciled the data stage by stage, the agent designs I had to invert after the first version: each felt like a setback while it was happening and like progress afterward.

Arnold Glasow’s line on my list puts it well: “you get the chicken by hatching the egg, not by smashing it.” Forcing faster progress usually produces shallow understanding that collapses under pressure. Giving myself time to learn properly, while keeping the work consistent, has produced more durable skills than any burst of intensity. Patience with myself turns out to be a performance strategy, not just a kindness. It is how I expect to keep improving in both fields for years.

title: Building the Platform I Wanted to Use
body:
Alan Kay said, “The best way to predict the future is to invent it.” It is one of the building quotes on my list, and it explains why Outsette exists. Outsette is a student intelligence platform live at its own domain, with AI-curated daily briefings, an opportunity tracker for internships and roles, an AI career advisor and club events, backed by real accounts and a production pipeline.

It is aimed at a problem I know firsthand. As a student looking for opportunities in finance and AI, the roles, events and news that matter are scattered across too many sources. I could have waited for a school or a company to build a better tool. Kay’s line pushed me toward the other option: if the thing I need does not exist yet, building it is often faster than waiting.

Building it also taught me things I could not have learned from coursework. Real accounts mean authentication and data that has to be handled responsibly. A daily briefing means a pipeline that runs every day whether or not I am paying attention. Users arrive with expectations that no assignment ever set. Each of those constraints made the platform harder to build and made me a better builder.

I think students have more power to invent than they assume. We are close to the problems students face, we have time to experiment and the tools to build working products have never been more accessible. The future of how students find opportunities will be shaped by someone. Kay’s line is a reminder that it might as well be people who actually feel the problem every day. Outsette is my attempt to take that seriously, one daily briefing at a time.
